The heaviest of the sans alphabets

Put the two bolds beside each other and the difference is the serifs, not the weight. Serif bold has feet and modulated strokes; the sans-serif bold run at U+1D5D4 is a plain heavy letter with nothing on the ends, which makes it the blackest thing in the block once the size drops. Its digits sit at U+1D7EC, so a number inside a heading holds the same weight as the words on either side of it.

A pinned announcement, a list header, a section label buried in a long description: anywhere a plain-text field gives you no headings of its own, one line of this supplies one. Restraint matters more here than with the lighter styles, since a full paragraph is tiring to read, and on a device that lacks the block every letter becomes an empty rectangle rather than degrading to something legible.

Where Sans-Serif Bold text works, and where it does not

WorksWorks in most bios, posts, display names and chat — X, Instagram, TikTok, Discord, Reddit. Watch outRefused by real-name fields (Facebook, LinkedIn's name field) and unsearchable: these are separate characters from ordinary letters, so nobody will find you by typing your name.

Sans-Serif Bold questions

How does this differ from the serif bold generator?

Only in the letterforms. Both are complete bold alphabets with their own digits, encoded in the same block. Serif bold has bracketed feet and thick-to-thin strokes, which reads as traditional; sans-serif bold is uniform and blunt, which reads as an interface heading. Pick whichever matches the text it will sit next to.

Can I mix it with normal typing in one line?

Yes, and that is usually the right way to use it. Since these are just characters, you can paste three styled words at the front of a plain sentence and get a heading and body in a field that supports neither. Keep the searchable words in plain letters.

Will text in this style show up in search?

Not under its plain spelling. A search engine or a site search matches the characters it was given, and a bold sans A is not the letter A, so the word is effectively invisible to anyone typing normally. Anything that needs to be found should appear somewhere in ordinary letters as well.
